newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Confident EU sets sights on millenium.
newsitem.headline: Confident EU sets sights on millenium.

text.p: The European Union, confident plans for a single currency are on track, has renewed a pledge to reform itself for the other great challenge of the millenium -- embracing new members in east Europe and the Mediterranean.
A special summit in Dublin on Saturday achieved its modest ambition of making leaders reaffirm a commitment to wrap up negotiations for a new treaty by the middle of 1997.
"Like cyclists going up a hill, we have decided to get out of the saddle and pedal harder," Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar said afterwards.

The leaders hope that their public vows will allow negotiators at their treaty review, known as the inter-governmental conference (IGC), to begin the hard bargaining needed to prepare the 15-nation bloc to take in up to a dozen newcomers, ranging from Malta to Poland.
"Today's institutions will not work in a community of 20, 25, 27 countries," said European Commission President Jacques Santer.

For some, the answer is obvious. The IGC must lead to more decisions by majority voting, less use of the veto, and a flexible structure which allows some countries to move ahead without waiting for the others.

But others such as British Prime Minister John Major, whose flagging Conservative government is deeply hostile to further moves towards traditional EU integration, would prefer to see a looser union based around strong, independent nations.
Major again criticised his colleagues for moving too quickly without thought for the consequences.
"Look before you leap is a much better watchword for the EU than leap before you look," he told reporters.

And all leaders were reminded that their last ambitious reform, the Maastricht Treaty agreed almost five years ago that set out the path to monetary union and further integration, almost foundered on the rock of public opposition.
"Without transparency, without efficiency, without internal security, we will not see the support from ordinary people for the outcome of the IGC," Santer said.
"We must constantly realise that the result...must be ratified by means of a referendum in a number of member states."

Leaders were at pains to deny they were scaling down their ambitions, after speculation prompted by German Chancellor Helmut Kohl's comments that more reforms would be needed to EU institutions even after the current treaty talks.

Kohl said reports that this meant he wanted a postponement of the IGC were "absurd". He said he had meant that five or 10 years after the new treaty was approved there might be a need for more revisions.

Kohl and French President Jacques Chirac both said there had been substantial support among the leaders to reinforce joint foreign policy decision-making among the bloc's members and improve action to fight crime, drugs and terrorism.
Both were clear on the consequences of failure.
"If there is a failure...this will be carried over to enlargement," French President Jacques Chirac told reporters. German Chancellor Helmut Kohl said delay in the talks would be "very dangerous".
In other decisions, the summit decided to send Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring to the Middle East to offer the bloc's help in the peace process between Israelis and Palestinians.
It was in part a reflection of the frustration of the bloc, which is the main financer of peace in the region, at being left out of U.S.-led peace moves.

Over an informal dinner at the end of the talks -- but without Major, who had to return to London to prepare for his party conference next week -- the leaders discussed relations with the United States, Russia and eastern Europe.
